Apex Industrial Technologies Inc. - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Industrial Technologies Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to press star one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star two. Please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Jordan Lee, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Jordan Lee (Vice President of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Apex Industrial Technologies' results for the Q3 2024. Joining me on today's call are Mark Harlan, Chief Executive Officer; Emily Carter, Chief Financial Officer; Raj Singh, Chief Operating Officer; and Dr. Elena Vasquez, Chief Technology Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Mark Harlan.

Mark Harlan (CEO):
Thank you, Jordan, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on Apex Industrial Technologies' performance for the Q3. We've made significant progress on several fronts, particularly in navigating supply chain headwinds, labor shortages, and the shift toward Industry 4.0 and electrification while executing disciplined M&A, capitalizing on demand trends in construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing, delivering strong operating margins across segments, maintaining solid order intake and backlog conversion, investing strategically in capex, managing price-cost dynamics effectively, and addressing supply chain constraints head-on. We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Emily Carter to provide more detail on our financial results.

Emily Carter (CFO):
Thank you, Mark. Turning to our financial performance, Apex Industrial Technologies reported $2.8 billion in revenue for the quarter, representing a 15% increase year-over-year. Gross margin was 28.7%, driven by favorable pricing actions, operational efficiencies from our digital transformation efforts, and a richer mix of high-margin aftermarket services. Operating expenses were $350 million, resulting in an operating income of $550 million. Our net income for the quarter was $420 million, or $1.85 per share.

We are committed to maintaining a strong balance sheet and generating consistent cash flow, with free cash flow conversion exceeding 90% and net debt-to-EBITDA at a healthy 1.8 times.

As we wrap up our Q3 results, I'd like to dive deeper into several key areas starting with our M&A activity, which continues to be a cornerstone of our strategy to drive long-term value in the industrial equipment sector. In an industry facing persistent supply chain headwinds, labor shortages, and the accelerating shift toward Industry 4.0 and electrification, we've been disciplined yet opportunistic—completing two bolt-on acquisitions year-to-date for a total enterprise value of $450 million, while divesting a non-core legacy asset. This positions us strongly for accretive growth, with expected synergies of $65 million annually by year three, at an average EBITDA multiple of 8.2x, well below our weighted average cost of capital.

Let me start with our most recent deal: the $320 million acquisition of TechForge Robotics, a leader in collaborative robot arms—or cobots—announced last month and expected to close in Q4. TechForge brings best-in-class precision automation solutions, including their TF-500 series cobots optimized for high-mix, low-volume manufacturing lines, which integrate seamlessly with our existing FANUC-inspired CNC machining centers and Siemens-style PLC controls. Strategically, this addresses the acute labor shortage in the sector—U.S. manufacturing PMI surveys show skilled labor gaps widening to 15% of capacity utilization—and taps into the $25 billion global cobot TAM growing at 28% CAGR through 2028, per McKinsey data.

The rationale here is multifaceted. First, product portfolio expansion: TechForge's software stack, featuring AI-driven adaptive learning algorithms for real-time path optimization, enhances our digital twin capabilities via our proprietary iMach platform. We're already piloting integrations at key customer sites like Tesla's Gigafactory Nevada and Intel's Fab 52 in Arizona, where cobot uptime has improved 22% in beta tests. This creates immediate cross-sell opportunities into our installed base of 45,000 machine tools globally, targeting a 15% attach rate uplift.

Second, geographic diversification: TechForge's 40% revenue from APAC—primarily serving semiconductor fabs in Taiwan and South Korea—bolsters our regional mix. APAC now represents 32% of our pro forma revenue, up from 25% pre-deal, as we capitalize on the CHIPS Act-fueled $52 billion U.S. reshoring wave and TSMC's $65 billion Arizona investment. In Europe, where EU Green Deal mandates are driving 12% YoY demand for electrified equipment, TechForge's IP69K-rated cobots align perfectly with battery gigafactory builds by Northvolt and VW.

Financially, this is highly accretive: $120 million in trailing twelve-month revenue at 25% margins, adding 75 basis points to EPS in year one post-synergies. Cost savings of $25 million stem from shared procurement—leveraging our scale in rare earth magnets and servo motors—and G&A overlap. We've structured it with 60% cash and 40% stock to preserve our net debt-to-EBITDA at 1.8x.

Complementing this was our $130 million tuck-in acquisition of Precision Hydraulics in Q2, a specialist in electro-hydraulic actuators for heavy earthmoving equipment. This bolsters our hydraulic portfolio amid the electrification trend—think hybrid excavators akin to Caterpillar's 320 XE—where hydraulic efficiency gains of 18% reduce fuel consumption by 12%, per SAE standards. It counters cyclicality in mining and construction, segments down 8% YoY due to commodity price softness, by diversifying into renewables like offshore wind turbine installation gear.

On the divestiture front, we sold our underperforming North American stamping press line for $75 million—generating a $20 million gain—to streamline focus on high-growth automation. This non-core asset had been dragging returns at 6% ROIC versus our 18% hurdle.

Looking ahead, our M&A pipeline remains robust at $2.5 billion, targeting 4-6 deals over the next 18 months. Priorities include platform acquisitions in factory IoT software—echoing Rockwell Automation's PTC ThingWorx play—and advanced materials for semiconductor etch tools, given ASML and Applied Materials' capex surge. We're eyeing Europe for sustainability tech, like carbon-neutral forging presses, to meet Scope 3 emissions targets, and India for localization amid PLI scheme incentives projecting $10 billion in electronics manufacturing equipment demand.

In summary, our M&A engine is firing on all cylinders: revenue synergies at 4-6% of deal value, disciplined multiples, and a clear path to 12-15% organic-plus-M&A growth. This isn't just financial engineering—it's about owning the automation megatrend in a $450 billion addressable market.

Next, I'll cover demand dynamics across our core end markets—construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing—which collectively represent about 85% of our equipment sales and 70% of our parts and services revenue. Overall, we saw robust demand in Q3, with total bookings up 12% year-over-year to $2.8 billion, driving our backlog to a record $18.5 billion, up 15% from last year. This reflects a healthy multi-year capex cycle, though we're mindful of moderating interest rates and softening commodity prices in some areas. Regionally, North America remains our growth engine at +18% bookings growth, fueled by infrastructure tailwinds; EMEA is flat-to-up 3% amid energy transition investments; APAC grew 8%, led by India and Southeast Asia; while LATAM dipped 2% due to agricultural headwinds in Brazil.

In construction, which is 42% of Q3 equipment sales, demand is firing on all cylinders, with global construction equipment shipments up an estimated 7% year-over-year per off-highway research from firms like AED and ITCAD. In North America, we're benefiting immensely from the IIJA's $1.2 trillion infrastructure pipeline—highway, bridge, and broadband projects are driving excavator and wheel loader orders, where we captured 22% market share with our new 350-ton XE-series electric excavators. Housing starts may be soft at 1.35 million annualized units, but non-residential is booming, including data center builds for hyperscalers like AWS and Google, which require our compact telehandlers and rough-terrain forklifts. Bookings in this segment rose 16% to $1.2 billion, with aftermarket parts up 11% on higher utilization rates averaging 75%. Europe is challenged by high energy costs, but we're seeing pockets of strength in wind farm foundations. Strategically, we've ramped production at our Peoria facility by 20% for autonomous dozers, integrating Caterpillar-like Command tech with our own AI-driven grade control, targeting a 15% margin uplift from digital services by 2025.

Mining, at 28% of equipment sales, remains a standout, with demand underpinned by elevated copper prices at $4.50/lb and lithium at $15,000/tonne, driven by electrification megatrends. Global mining capex is projected at $140 billion for 2024 by Wood Mackenzie, up 5%, and our ultra-class haul trucks and autonomous shuttle trains are at the epicenter. We booked $850 million in Q3, +14% YoY, including a landmark $200 million order from a major copper producer in Chile for our 400-ton battery-electric haulers, akin to Komatsu's e-dumper but with our proprietary fast-charge tech reducing downtime by 30%. Backlog here is $5.2 billion, providing 2.5 years of visibility. Regionally, Australia and Canada are strong (+12%), but Indonesia's nickel boom is accelerating with our hybrid drills. Aftermarket is thriving at +9% growth, as fleets age into replacement cycles—average truck age now 8 years. Our initiative? A $150 million R&D push into teleremote mining systems, partnering with Hexagon for digital twins that optimize ore throughput by 10-15%, positioning us for the $50 billion autonomous mining opportunity by 2030.

Agriculture, representing 18% of equipment sales, is more mixed, reflecting volatile farm incomes and destocking. US farm cash receipts are flat at $185 billion per USDA, but precision ag adoption is a bright spot. Our tractors and combines saw 4% bookings growth to $520 million, led by North America's high-horsepower segment—think 400+ HP models like our updated 8R series with John Deere-inspired AutoTrac guidance, which boosted dealer inventories to healthy levels without excess. Row-crop demand is solid, up 6% on corn/soy yields, but Brazil's sugar cane and soy weakness shaved 5% off LATAM volumes amid El Niño recovery. Europe faces subsidy cuts, but our compact utility tractors are gaining in dairy regions. Aftermarket parts grew 7%, supported by telematics uptake—over 60% of our fleet now connected via our Precision Ag platform, driving $100 million in recurring software revenue. Strategically, we're leaning into electrification with beta tests of 100 HP electric tractors for orchards, targeting EU Green Deal compliance, and expanding sprayer capacity in Iowa by 25% to capture the $10 billion global precision planting market.

Manufacturing, at 12% of equipment sales, demand is accelerating on reshoring and automation waves. US factory output rose 2.5% YoY per ISM, with semiconductors and EVs leading—think Intel's Ohio fab and Tesla's Texas gigafactory expansions requiring our overhead cranes and AGVs. Bookings hit $280 million, +22% YoY, including material handling gear for battery plants. APAC, particularly Vietnam and India, is reshoring magnets, up 15%. Backlog stands at $2.1 billion. We're capitalizing with our next-gen AMR (autonomous mobile robots) integrated with Rockwell Automation PLCs, reducing labor costs by 20%. Aftermarket services are up 13% on IoT predictive maintenance.

Looking ahead, we expect 8-10% organic growth in 2025 across these markets, with construction and mining offsetting any ag softness. Risks include China stimulus delays and potential Fed cuts curbing capex, but our $1.2 billion share repurchase and 15% dividend hike signal confidence. Key initiatives: $500 million in capex for US and India factories, focusing on modular electrification platforms to cut development costs 25%; M&A pipeline targeting aftermarket software like Uptake; and sustainability goals—30% emissions reduction via hybrid fleets by 2027. We're well-positioned in this fragmented $250 billion industry, with ROIC at 22% and free cash flow conversion over 90%.

Before moving on, good afternoon, everyone. I'd like to dive deep into our operating margin performance by segment. Overall, we delivered a consolidated operating margin of 14.2% this quarter, up 120 basis points year-over-year and 50 basis points sequentially from Q2. This marks our strongest quarterly margin in the past five years, driven by a mix of favorable product pricing, operational efficiencies from our Apex 4.0 digital transformation initiative, and robust demand across our core end-markets. However, we continue to navigate headwinds like raw material inflation—particularly steel and aluminum, which rose 8% YoY—and supply chain disruptions in semiconductors for our automation lines.

Our four reporting segments: Heavy Machinery, Automation & Robotics, Energy Equipment, and Precision Components.

Heavy Machinery Segment (42% of Revenue): This segment, which includes our earthmoving equipment like large mining trucks and hydraulic excavators akin to Caterpillar's 793F haulers, posted an operating margin of 16.8%—up from 14.9% a year ago and expanding 90 basis points sequentially. Revenue grew 12% YoY to $1.2 billion, fueled by a book-to-bill ratio of 1.3x and a backlog now exceeding $4.5 billion.

Margin expansion was propelled by several factors: First, pricing actions added 250 basis points, as we passed through 6-7% list price increases on new orders amid sticky commodity costs. Second, our lean manufacturing programs at our Peoria, Illinois, and Monterrey, Mexico facilities boosted capacity utilization to 92%, up from 85% last year, reducing variable COGS per unit by 4%. We're leveraging predictive maintenance via IoT sensors—similar to Komatsu's Komtrax system—which cut unplanned downtime by 22%.

Regionally, North America drove 55% of growth, benefiting from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, with strong OEM demand from aggregates and construction. APAC was mixed: China softness in property development shaved 20 bps off margins, but India and Australia mining ramp-ups offset this, with iron ore majors like Rio Tinto awarding us multi-year frame agreements. Europe faced FX headwinds from a stronger USD, compressing margins by 30 bps, but reshoring trends post-Ukraine supply shocks are building momentum.

Automation & Robotics Segment (28% of Revenue): Here, margins reached 13.5%, a robust 180 basis point YoY improvement from 11.7%, though flat sequentially due to R&D ramp on next-gen cobots. Revenue hit $785 million, up 15% YoY, with shipments of our FANUC-like articulated robots surging on automotive retooling.

Key drivers included SG&A leverage—down to 8.2% of sales from 9.5%—and supply chain optimizations via our Vendor Managed Inventory program with key suppliers like Rockwell Automation partners. We absorbed a 10% YoY chip shortage premium but mitigated it through dual-sourcing in Taiwan and Malaysia, preserving 150 bps of margin. Our Industry 4.0 digital twin platform, rolled out across 15 factories, improved throughput by 18%, directly flowing to the bottom line.

North America led with 18% growth from EV battery gigafactory builds by clients like Tesla and GM, where our palletizing systems are integral. EMEA margins expanded 200 bps on semiconductor fab expansions in Germany, echoing ASML's ecosystem boom. APAC, at 60% of segment revenue, saw Vietnam and Indonesia offset China's COVID lockdowns, though we're monitoring U.S.-China tariffs that could add 50 bps pressure next year.

Energy Equipment Segment (18% of Revenue): Margins here came in at 12.1%, up 90 bps YoY from 11.2% but down 40 bps sequentially on seasonal LNG maintenance cycles. Revenue of $510 million grew 9% YoY, led by turbine components and wind gear boxes comparable to Siemens Gamesa's offerings.

Performance benefited from our electrification pivot: 25% of orders now feature hybrid drivetrains, capturing renewables tailwinds under the Inflation Reduction Act. We clawed back 120 bps via value engineering—redesigning compressor housings to shave 5% aluminum content—and energy surcharges on 70% of contracts. However, upstream oil & gas volatility, with Brent at $85/barrel, tempered aftermarket parts uptake.

U.S. shale producers like ExxonMobil drove 45% of revenue, with margins at 14% thanks to Permian Basin frac pump demand. Europe surged 22% on Nord Stream replacement urgency and offshore wind farms in the North Sea, boosting regional margins to 13.5%. Middle East & Africa held steady at 11%, pressured by OPEC+ cuts, but our strategic JV with Aramco for hydrogen-ready turbines positions us for 20% growth in 2025.

Precision Components Segment (12% of Revenue): This high-mix, low-volume segment delivered 10.4% margins, expanding 140 bps YoY from 9.0% and 60 bps sequentially. Revenue rose 11% to $340 million, anchored by CNC machining for aerospace fasteners and medical devices.

Margin gains stemmed from our Advanced Manufacturing Excellence (AME) initiative, deploying 3D-printed tooling that cut setup times by 35%, akin to GE Additive's approach. We also optimized our global footprint, idling underutilized lines in legacy U.S. plants and ramping in low-cost Mexico hubs, saving 200 bps in labor costs. Raw material hedging locked in copper and titanium at 2022 lows, shielding us from 15% spot inflation.

Aerospace OEMs like Boeing and Airbus, ramping 737 MAX and A320neo production, fueled 60% growth, with aftermarket MRO up 25%. North America margins hit 12%, Europe 11% amid Airbus supply chain snarls, and APAC steady at 9% on commercial aviation recovery in India.

Across segments, our focus on operational discipline—targeting 85%+ capacity utilization enterprise-wide—and pricing discipline has decoupled margins from topline volatility, even as steel tariffs and logistics costs linger. We're investing $250 million in FY25 capex for AI-driven quality control and sustainable manufacturing, aiming for carbon-neutral factories by 2030 to meet Scope 3 demands from customers like John Deere.

Looking forward, we expect Q4 consolidated margins of 14.5-15.0%, with Heavy Machinery leading expansion. Risks include prolonged China weakness and potential U.S. recession hitting capex, but our $7.2 billion backlog and 1.25x book-to-bill provide visibility. We're well-positioned in megatrends like electrification, automation, and reshoring, mirroring peers like Honeywell and Illinois Tool Works.

Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. This is Emily Carter speaking, and I'll dive into our order intake expectations and backlog conversion rates for Q3, providing some color on the trends we're seeing across our Manufacturing and Industrial Equipment segments. As you know, order intake is a leading indicator for our business—it's the fuel for our revenue engine—while backlog conversion rates give us clear visibility into execution and cash flow generation. I'll tie this back to our strategic priorities in automation, precision machining, and sustainable manufacturing solutions, where we're positioned against peers like Haas Automation, DMG Mori, and Fanuc in CNC systems and robotics.

Starting with Q3 order intake: We booked $1.28 billion, up 18% year-over-year and 5% sequentially from Q2. This exceeded our guidance midpoint of $1.15 to $1.25 billion, driven primarily by strength in our high-margin automation and material handling equipment lines. Book-to-bill came in at 1.12x, reflecting robust demand from end-markets like semiconductors and electric vehicle battery production. Notably, our FANUC-compatible robotic arms and collaborative robots (cobots) saw a 32% YoY surge, fueled by labor shortages and Industry 4.0 upgrades—think customers like Intel fabs and Tesla Gigafactories automating their lines.

Regionally, North America was the standout at 42% of intake, up 25% YoY on reshoring tailwinds under the CHIPS Act and Inflation Reduction Act. We're seeing capex cycles accelerate in U.S. discrete manufacturing, with orders for our modular CNC lathes and 5-axis mills from aerospace primes like Boeing suppliers. Europe contributed 28%, flat YoY but with sequential improvement as energy costs stabilize post-Ukraine crisis; German OEMs in automotive are cautiously ramping for next-gen EV stamping presses. Asia-Pacific was 25%, down 5% YoY due to China's ongoing property sector drag, but offset by a 40% jump in semiconductor equipment orders from TSMC and Samsung ecosystem players. Emerging markets like India rounded out at 5%, with early wins in steel mill revamps.

Looking forward, our full-year order intake guidance is $5.0 to $5.4 billion, implying 12-20% growth over 2023. For Q4, we expect $1.25 to $1.35 billion, weighted toward the higher end if U.S. industrial production holds above 2% YoY as per ISM data. Risks here include potential softening in China construction equipment—our hydraulic excavator attachments are exposed—but we're mitigating with diversification into renewables, where wind turbine tower welding systems are gaining traction.

Shifting to backlog: We ended Q3 at $3.7 billion, up 14% YoY and providing 14-16 months of revenue visibility at current run rates. This is a healthy mix: 55% in automation and precision tools (quick-turn, high-velocity), 30% in heavy industrial presses and forging equipment (longer-lead), and 15% in aftermarket upgrades like our IoT-enabled predictive maintenance kits. Customer concentration remains disciplined—top 10 at 28% of backlog, diversified across 450 active accounts.

On conversion rates, this is where our operational excellence shines. Q3 backlog-to-revenue conversion was 28%, up from 24% a year ago and above our long-term target of 25-27%. This improvement stems from three key initiatives: Supply chain resilience—post-2022 disruptions, we've localized 70% of critical components like servo motors and linear guides to North American and European suppliers, reducing lead times from 20 weeks to 12. Our dual-sourcing with names like Yaskawa and Bosch has de-risked volatility in rare earths for EV-related gear drives. Digital transformation: Rollout of digital twins and AI-driven shop floor optimization across our 15 global factories has boosted throughput by 15%. For instance, in our Ohio CNC plant, we're converting Haas VF-series equivalents 10% faster via generative design software that simulates part flow pre-production. Modular platform strategy: 60% of new orders are now on our "FlexForge" modular architecture—scalable presses and handlers that cut customization time by 30%. This is particularly accretive in aerospace, where Boeing 737 MAX tooling conversions are converting at 32% quarterly rates.

Trailing 12-month conversion now stands at 105% of book-to-bill, validating our pricing power amid steel and aluminum inflation (up 8% YoY per LME indices). We expect Q4 at 27-29%, with full-year averaging 27%, supporting our raised FY24 revenue guide of $9.8 to $10.2 billion.

Strategically, these metrics underscore our pivot toward high-growth adjacencies: We're targeting 25% of 2025 intake from green tech, like hydrogen electrolyzer skids and solar tracker actuators, capitalizing on IRA subsidies. Margins benefit too—automation backlog carries 28% incremental EBITDA versus 22% for legacy equipment—positioning us for 150-200bps expansion.

Good afternoon, everyone. As we look ahead, our capital expenditure—or CapEx—strategy remains a cornerstone of our long-term value creation in the industrial equipment sector. We're laser-focused on driving sustainable growth amid a dynamic market landscape, including persistent supply chain headwinds, the ongoing push toward Industry 4.0, and accelerating demand for electrified and automated solutions.

For fiscal 2024, we're guiding to total CapEx of $450 million, representing a 15% increase from our $390 million spend in FY2023. This elevation reflects our confidence in a robust order backlog—now standing at $3.2 billion, up 22% year-over-year—and targeted ROIC expansion to above 12% on new investments. We've maintained disciplined capital allocation, with approximately 70% of our CapEx directed toward growth initiatives that deliver payback periods under 3 years, while the balance supports maintenance and regulatory compliance. Importantly, these projects are all NPV-positive at our 10% hurdle rate, even in conservative steel price scenarios where hot-rolled coil benchmarks hover around $800 per ton.

Our priorities are aligned with four strategic pillars: capacity expansion, digital transformation and automation, sustainability upgrades, and R&D innovation.

First, capacity expansion—accounting for 40% of our CapEx, or $180 million. We're prioritizing buildouts to meet surging demand in material handling and precision machining segments. A key initiative is the $120 million greenfield expansion at our Peoria, Illinois facility, which will add 250,000 square feet of manufacturing space dedicated to next-gen electric forklifts and autonomous guided vehicles (AGVs). This mirrors trends we've seen at peers like Crown Equipment and Toyota Industries, where EV adoption in warehousing is growing at 25% CAGR through 2028, per McKinsey data. We'll ramp production here by Q4 2025, targeting an incremental $250 million in annual revenue at 20% EBITDA margins. Regionally, this U.S.-centric investment supports reshoring efforts under the CHIPS Act and Inflation Reduction Act, capturing onshoring from Asia amid U.S. tariffs on steel imports now at 25%.

In Europe, we're allocating $40 million to debottleneck our Dortmund plant, focusing on CNC lathes and milling machines for the automotive OEMs like Volkswagen and Stellantis. This responds to the EU's Green Deal mandates, where demand for high-precision equipment is up 18% YoY due to EV battery production ramps.

Second, digital transformation and automation—30% of CapEx, or $135 million. Labor shortages and margin pressures are pushing the industry toward smart factories, and we're ahead of the curve. $80 million is earmarked for retrofitting our six core plants with IoT-enabled systems, including Siemens MindSphere platforms and our proprietary ApexAI predictive maintenance suite. This builds on our pilot at the Dayton site, where downtime has dropped 35% and OEE improved to 92%. Expect $50 million in annual savings by 2026 from reduced scrap rates—now under 1.5%—and optimized throughput.

We're also investing $55 million in collaborative robotics (cobots) integration, partnering with Universal Robots for lines producing hydraulic presses and welding systems. This addresses the 15% skilled labor gap highlighted in Deloitte's 2024 Manufacturing Outlook, positioning us competitively against Honeywell and Rockwell Automation.

Third, sustainability initiatives—20% of CapEx, or $90 million. Decarbonization isn't optional; it's a competitive moat. $60 million will fund solar arrays and heat pump retrofits across our U.S. and European footprint, targeting a 25% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2027—aligning with SBTi commitments. At our expanded Peoria site, we're installing 5 MW of on-site solar, slashing energy costs by 18% amid $0.12/kWh industrial rates. Additionally, $30 million goes to R&D for low-emission powder metallurgy processes in our gear manufacturing, reducing CO2 intensity by 40% compared to traditional forging. This taps into ESG-driven procurement from customers like John Deere and Caterpillar, where green premiums are boosting order wins by 12%.

Finally, R&D and maintenance—10% of CapEx, or $45 million. We're doubling down on hydrogen-ready fuel cell tech for off-road equipment, with $25 million toward prototypes that could disrupt diesel dominance, akin to Cummins' advancements. The rest ensures our asset base remains modern, with fleet utilization at 95%.

Regionally, North America gets 55% of spend ($248 million) for reshoring tailwinds; EMEA 25% ($113 million) for regulatory-driven growth; and Asia-Pacific 20% ($90 million), including a $40 million line expansion in Chennai for semiconductor fab tools amid TSMC's India push. We expect these investments to drive free cash flow growth to $600 million in FY2025, up from $480 million this year, with CapEx moderating to 4-5% of sales thereafter.

As we dive into the financials further, I'd like to spend some time on our price-cost dynamics, which were a key driver behind our gross margin expansion this quarter. We delivered adjusted gross margins of 28.7%, up 180 basis points sequentially from Q2 and 110 basis points year-over-year. This marks our third consecutive quarter of margin expansion, bringing us back toward our pre-pandemic normalized range of 29-30%.

First, on the cost side. Raw material inflation remained a persistent challenge, though it's showing signs of moderation. Steel, which represents about 35% of our COGS in our core earthmoving and material handling segments—like our APX-500 excavators and conveyor systems—saw spot prices rise 4% sequentially per the CRU North America index, driven by lingering supply constraints from U.S. mill maintenance turnarounds at players like Nucor and Steel Dynamics. Year-over-year, steel is up 12%, but we've seen destocking in the channel help offset some of that. Aluminum, critical for our lightweight automation equipment such as the ApexBot robotic arms, ticked up 2% QoQ on LME, but declined 3% YoY amid softer Chinese exports. Copper, key for electrification components in our power generation lineup, surged 6% sequentially due to U.S. infrastructure spending pull-forward, echoing trends we've seen at peers like Cummins in their genset business.

Beyond metals, we had freight and logistics costs up 5% QoQ, though ocean rates from Asia have stabilized post-Panama Canal disruptions. Labor inflation in our U.S. and Mexico facilities added another 3% pressure, with skilled welders and CNC machinists commanding 7-8% wage hikes. All-in, input costs rose about 3.5% sequentially, or roughly $45 million headwind on a run-rate basis for our $2.8 billion quarterly revenue.

Now, turning to pricing—where we demonstrated strong commercial discipline. We realized full passthrough on 85% of our exposed volumes through a combination of list price increases, surcharges, and index-linked escalators. In Q3, we executed targeted pricing actions averaging 5.2% across our portfolio: 6% on heavy equipment like our hydraulic presses and stamping lines sold into automotive OEMs; 4.5% on precision machining tools for aerospace; and 5.8% on our energy-efficient CNC lathes, where customers like Boeing and GE Vernova accepted hikes tied to productivity gains from our IoT-enabled ApexLink software suite.

Customer acceptance was robust, particularly in North America, where backlog visibility—now at 14 months, up from 11 in Q2—gave us leverage. We saw minimal pushback, with order cancellation rates under 2%, comparable to Deere & Company's recent quarters. In Europe, pricing realization was softer at 3.8% due to energy cost passthrough resistance amid the Ukraine-related gas crisis, but we mitigated via selective surcharges on high-margin castings. Asia-Pacific, representing 22% of sales, benefited from a favorable mix shift toward higher-ASP semiconductor fab equipment, where we captured 7% pricing on cleanroom wafer handlers.

Net-net, pricing more than offset cost inflation by 220 basis points, delivering that 180 bps gross margin beat. On an absolute basis, this added $62 million to gross profit versus our internal models. Mix was a tailwind too—favoring 45% higher-margin aftermarket parts and services, which grew 12% YoY and carry 50%+ margins, insulated by our dealer network akin to Caterpillar's model.

Strategically, we're not resting on our laurels. We've ramped our hedging program to 60% coverage on steel and aluminum for FY24, using LME and CME futures to lock in floors at current levels. Supply chain diversification is accelerating: 25% of our castings now sourced from low-cost Mexico facilities via our new Monterrey plant, reducing China exposure from 18% to 12%. Value engineering initiatives—like redesigning our APX-400 forklifts with high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steel—shaved 2.5% off material intensity without compromising specs. And we're embedding AI-driven cost forecasting in our ERP system, partnering with Siemens for predictive analytics on Platts indices.

Regionally, North America remains our margin fortress at 32% gross margins, fueled by onshoring in semiconductors and EVs—think TSMC's Arizona fab ordering our wafer polishers. Europe is at 24%, pressured by 20%+ energy costs, but our €50 million green steel initiative with ThyssenKrupp positions us for EU CBAM compliance. APAC margins hit 27%, with India up 300 bps on localization for our tractor attachments serving Mahindra.

Looking ahead to Q4 and FY24, we expect price-cost to remain accretive by 100-150 bps. We'll layer on another 4-5% pricing early next year, targeting 90% realization, while input costs moderate to 1-2% inflation assuming no major geopolitical flares. This supports our raised FY24 gross margin guidance to 28.5% and EBITDA margins of 15.2%. We're well-positioned in this cycle, leveraging our 40% market share in North American material handling to drive shareholder value.

Good afternoon, everyone. Before I dive into the segment results more broadly, I want to provide a detailed update on our supply chain dynamics, as these continue to be a key focus for investors and a critical driver of our operational performance in the industrial equipment sector. As you know, Apex Industrial Technologies designs and manufactures heavy-duty CNC machining centers, automated assembly lines, and precision hydraulic systems for industries like automotive, aerospace, and renewable energy. Our bill of materials—or BOM—is heavily weighted toward high-precision components such as semiconductors for PLCs and HMIs, forged steel castings, rare earth magnets for servo motors, and specialized alloys for hydraulic cylinders.

We've made meaningful progress in mitigating the supply chain headwinds that plagued us through 2023, but we're not out of the woods yet. Global lead times for critical components have improved by 35% quarter-over-quarter, averaging 18 weeks now versus a peak of 28 weeks in Q4 '23. This has allowed us to reduce our backlog conversion delays from 12 weeks to just 6 weeks on average for our flagship TitanPro CNC series. However, component availability remains uneven, with cost inflation running at 12% year-over-year across our supply base—down from 22% last year—primarily driven by persistent volatility in electronics and metals.

Breaking it down by key categories: Electronics and Semiconductors (42% of BOM): This remains our toughest area. Shortages in automotive-grade microcontrollers and power semiconductors, exacerbated by lingering effects from the 2021-22 chip crunch and ongoing U.S.-China export restrictions on advanced nodes, have pushed our average procurement lead time to 22 weeks—still 50% above pre-pandemic norms. For context, we're sourcing from tier-1 suppliers like Infineon, NXP, and Texas Instruments, but allocation pressures on 300mm wafer fab capacity have limited our pulls. In Q3, this resulted in a 15% shortfall in HMI touch panels for our AutoLine assembly systems, contributing to $28 million in deferred revenue. Regionally, Asia-Pacific sourcing—70% of our semi needs—saw a 10% improvement thanks to TSMC's Arizona ramp-up, but European suppliers like STMicroelectronics are facing energy-driven delays from the Ukraine conflict spillover.

Metals and Castings (28% of BOM): Steel and aluminum pricing has stabilized somewhat, with hot-rolled coil benchmarks down 8% from Q2 peaks per S&P Global data. However, specialty alloys for our high-pressure hydraulic pumps—sourced from ArcelorMittal and Nucor—experienced 20-week lead times due to U.S. Midwest labor strikes and Red Sea shipping disruptions, which inflated ocean freight rates by 25% YoY. This hit our North American castings inventory turns, dropping from 8.2x to 6.5x. Positively, our European ops benefited from nearshoring gains, with lead times in Germany shortening to 12 weeks via Voestalpine partnerships.

Mechanical and Hydraulics (18% of BOM): Rare earths for permanent magnet motors remain a pain point, with neodymium prices up 18% amid Chinese export quotas. Bosch Rexroth and Parker Hannifin valves saw minor delays, but our strategic inventory build—now at 14 weeks of forward stock, up 25% YoY—shielded us from major disruptions. Inventory as a percentage of sales hit 22%, a deliberate hedge that's added $45 million to working capital but preserved our 98% on-time delivery rate for renewable energy skids.

Other Components (12% of BOM): Fasteners and belting are back to normal, but PCBAs for IoT-enabled controls face 10-15% cost creep from labor shortages in Mexico's maquiladoras.

Regionally, our commentary varies: In North America, which represents 55% of our revenue, U.S. reshoring incentives under the CHIPS Act have accelerated dual-sourcing, with 30% of our semi needs now fulfilled domestically or via Intel's Ohio fab. Europe, at 25% of sales, is challenged by EU carbon border taxes inflating alloy costs by 7%, but our Siemens collaboration on Industry 4.0 digitization has optimized routing. APAC, our 20% growth engine, benefits from Vietnam diversification but contends with Typhoon Gaemi-related port closures in recent months.

Strategically, we're not just reacting—we're transforming. We've launched a $150 million Supply Chain Resilience Initiative, including: Supplier Diversification—Onboarded 15 new tier-1 partners, reducing single-source dependency from 40% to 22% for top-20 components. For example, shifting 25% of hydraulic sourcing from China to India via Eaton's new Pune facility. Digital Twins and AI Forecasting: Rolled out SAP Ariba integrated with AI-driven demand sensing from Blue Yonder, improving forecast accuracy to 92% and cutting excess inventory by 18%. Vertical Integration: Acquired a 60,000 sq ft casting foundry in Indiana, targeting 40% self-sufficiency in alloy components by FY25, akin to Caterpillar's playbook. Nearshoring Push: Expanded Mexican capacity by 20% for CNC assemblies, slashing trans-Pacific transit risks.

Looking forward, we expect Q4 lead times to compress another 10-15% as Intel and TSMC ramps mature, with semi availability normalizing by year-end. Cost inflation should moderate to single digits, supporting our 8-10% gross margin expansion guidance. That said, we're conservatively baking in $20-30 million of potential upside revenue deferral if Red Sea tensions persist. Our book-to-bill remains strong at 1.3x, reflecting robust demand for automation gear amid the re-industrialization wave—think EV battery lines and wind turbine nacelles.

We're proud of our execution here; it's why we've outperformed peers like Deere and Honeywell on delivery metrics this quarter.
